subject: ecce
title: Early Identification and Intervention

sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: What is the purpose of early identification mentioned in the passage?
questions.answer: To determine which children have developmental problems that may be obstacles to learning or that place them at risk.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: ________ and ________ teachers play a crucial role in identifying developmental delays in young children.
questions.answer: Pre-school; kindergarten

questions.q: What should teachers do if they observe symptoms of developmental delay?
questions.answer: Share their observations and concerns with parents and other specialists.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: In early childhood, development is characterised by broad variability in ________ and ________ of maturation.
questions.answer: rates; patterns

questions.q: What is the challenge in the early identification of developmental problems in young children?
questions.answer: No clear distinction can yet be made between children whose problems will persist and those who will make adequate progress with time.

questions.q: Is every young child with early difficulties at risk for learning disabilities?
questions.answer: No — such children may or may not be at risk; but screening and support should still be given.

sections.passage: Pre-school and kindergarten teachers are at an advantageous position to catch the early signs and symptoms of a developmental delay or disability and to identify children who are at risk in learning and school. Teachers need to be aware of symptoms and share their observations and concerns with parents and other specialists. The purpose of early identification is to determine which children have developmental problems that may be obstacles to learning or that place children at risk. Development in early childhood years is characterised by broad variability in rates and patterns of maturation. At present, no clear distinction can be made in the early years between children whose problems may persist and those who will make adequate progress with time. Therefore, young children who demonstrate difficulties in early development may or may not be at risk for learning disabilities. (April 2024)

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Children with ________ issues may experience difficulty in responding to the regular forms of care and discipline. (ii) Many people with disabilities and their families have ________ awareness of assistive products and services.
questions.answer: (i) behavioural (ii) limited

questions.q: Answer in one sentence: As an ECCE teacher, mention one intervention you would take for a child having difficulty in reading and writing.
questions.answer: For example: give extra sound- and visual-discrimination games, rhymes and letter-sound matching in small steps with picture cards, observe the child systematically, share the concern with parents and refer the child to a special educator for assessment.
questions.note: The real question had three 1-mark parts; this part is from April 2026.

questions.q: State True or False: (i) Pre-school teachers are at a disadvantageous position to catch the early signs of a developmental delay. (ii) Development in early childhood years is characterised by broad variability in rates and patterns of maturation.
questions.answer: (i) False — they are at an advantageous position. (ii) True.

questions.q: Match: (a) Speech therapy (b) Developmentally appropriate intervention — (i) Speaking, eating and drinking skills (ii) An individual plan for each child (iii) Balance, sitting, crawling

Fill in the blanks: (i) ________ refers to an impairment of cognitive abilities that shows as a learning-related disability. (ii) Wheelchairs, scooters, walkers and canes are examples of ________ aids.
questions.answer: (i) Learning disability (ii) mobility

questions.q: Answer in one sentence: (i) What is screening? (ii) What are risk indicators?
questions.answer: (i) Determining the areas where children need assistance. (ii) Environmental, biological, genetic and prenatal conditions associated with adverse developmental outcomes — warning signs of a possible disability.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What are learning disabilities, and what is the biggest challenge for an ECCE teacher in identifying them?
questions.answer: A learning disability is an impairment of cognitive abilities that shows as difficulty in learning — in taking in, integrating, storing or expressing information. The biggest challenge is that learning disabilities are hard to identify and diagnose, since all young children make mistakes and development varies widely.

questions.q: Why is early identification of disabilities in children important? How can a teacher identify children with difficulty in reading and writing?
questions.answer: Early identification allows help while the young brain is most able to change, and greatly reduces later social, behavioural and learning difficulties. Signs of reading and writing difficulty: slow naming of objects and colours, weak rhyming and syllable blending, little interest in print, trouble learning letters and letter-sound connections.

questions.q: What intervention therapies can be used for children with disability?
questions.answer: Occupational therapy (fine motor, play and self-help skills like dressing and toileting), physiotherapy (balance, sitting, crawling, walking) and speech therapy (speech, language, eating and drinking), along with psychological services and special education.

questions.q: Who are children with disabilities?
questions.answer: Children with disabling health conditions or impairments — from birth or as a result of illness, poor nutrition or injury — who face limitations in activity and restrictions in participation, such as exclusion from school.
questions.note: April 2023 asked for a one-sentence explanation.

questions.q: Distinguish mental and psychological conditions from medical conditions.
questions.answer: Mental and psychological conditions affect the mind: intellectual disorders such as delayed mental development, and psychological disorders such as anxiety, chronic depression and mood swings. Medical conditions are weakening chronic physical illnesses such as heart disease, muscular dystrophy and cancer, with long periods of poor health, tests and hospital stays.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: What steps would you take to provide early intervention at an ECCE centre? Mention any three.
questions.answer: Any three: observe children systematically and screen them to find who needs help; share concerns with parents and refer the child for comprehensive evaluation by specialists; make an individual plan with the family and specialists and review it regularly; arrange therapy — occupational, physio or speech — and special educators; use child-focused strategies such as peer interaction, prompts, modelling and reinforcement in a supportive, structured, predictable environment; provide assistive devices and barrier-free access.

questions.q: Explain the developmentally appropriate characteristics of quality interventions.
questions.answer: A developmentally appropriate intervention is specially designed for children in relation to their disability; it has staff specially trained in the intervention and services they give; it develops an individual plan for each child and reviews it regularly; and it tracks the child's progress through regular assessments.

questions.q: How can assistive technologies support inclusion?
questions.answer: Assistive technology increases, maintains or improves the functioning of children with disabilities, helping them move (wheelchairs, walkers), hear (hearing aids), see and read (Braille, screen readers, enlargement software), communicate (communication boards) and take part in learning (pencil grips, book holders, ramps). It increases independence and participation in school, play and family life, can prevent secondary conditions, and lets children who cannot attend school learn from home through ICT.

questions.q: What are the barriers to easy access to assistive technologies?
questions.answer: Lack of awareness — many people with disabilities and their families know little about assistive products and services. Lack of governance — weak legislation, policies and national programmes; it is a low priority for many states. Lack of services — few services, often far from where children live. Lack of products — little or no production, with a small range of types, models and sizes.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Discuss the strategies for early identification of children with disabilities.
questions.answer: National policies, such as the National Policy for Persons with Disabilities (2006), ask that children up to six be identified at the earliest so they can join inclusive education at the right age. The process: (1) Screening — a system to identify, locate and evaluate children who need early intervention, finding the areas where they need help. (2) Risk indicators and protective factors — environmental, biological, genetic and prenatal conditions that warn of possible problems (but do not always predict them), weighed against protective factors such as special schools, educators and therapists that reduce risk and build resilience. (3) Systematic observation — informal or standard observations repeated over time at home, preschool and play, recording how often, how consistently and how severely the behaviour occurs. (4) Comprehensive evaluation — when risk is suspected, professionals evaluate periodically across settings and perspectives to find the child's pattern of abilities and needs and plan strategies and resources. Teachers should watch for warning signs in language, reading and writing, cognition, motor skills and social behaviour, and share them with parents.

questions.q: What is early intervention? Describe its advantages and the characteristics of quality interventions.
questions.answer: Early intervention means doing things as early as possible to work on a child's developmental, health and support needs, usually from birth to five, through services such as screening, speech, physical and occupational therapy, psychological, medical and nutrition services, home visits and social work. Advantages: better developmental, social and educational gains; less isolation, stress and frustration for families; fewer behaviour problems through positive strategies; children grow into productive, independent adults; lower future costs of special education and health care. Quality interventions are: family-centred — family works alongside professionals, flexible setting, support and guidance; developmentally appropriate — designed for the disability, trained staff, individual plans reviewed regularly, progress tracked; child-focused — practise skills in different settings, mix with peers; supportive and structured — a comfortable, well-organised, regular and predictable environment.
